div.head: Chapter 13
div.p: After this, the sixth part requires: the order of natural and divine law that the faith be preached by those who have made profession of it, and this according to the form that Christ established for us; that is to say, clearly and distinctly and explicitly, at length and with gentleness, as the Redeemer himself and his Apostles and those who conducted themselves thus converted the world.

The faith having been well preached, and the great majesty and divine power of the Vicar of Jesus Christ having been declared in the preaching, and the faith having been received by those simple and most gentle peoples, the seventh thing that the order of the aforesaid law must follow is that the very preachers of the Catholic faith, with great prudence, discretion, and industry, most gently and most sweetly, should persuade and induce the kings and lords and their peoples to receive them, of their own free and willing accord, almost as in gratitude for the great benefits received from the kings of Castile, who sent them preachers to give them the divine light and dispel the deep darkness in which they lived, as their universal and supreme princes; and thus, consenting to the said institution and promotion of the Vicar of Christ, with the natural kings and lords remaining in their own kingdoms and dominions which they previously possessed, setting before them the great utility and prosperity that would come to lords and subjects alike from having a Christian king as their superior.

The final thing required by natural and divine law, and no less necessary for the full justification and firmness of the supreme principality of our illustrious kings of Castile in the Indies, is that there be concluded, or ought to have been concluded, a certain treaty, convention, and pact or contract between Their Highnesses, or their officials in their name, and the natural kings of those lands and their peoples; on the part of the kings of Castile, promising to reign over and govern them justly and to preserve for them their states, their dignities, their laws and customs and liberties that are not and were not contrary to our faith or derogatory to the Christian religion, together with other reasonable conditions they might request. On the part of the native kings and lords and their kingdoms and peoples, they would offer freely, without any force or fear, all obedience, reverence, and fidelity to Their Highnesses and to their just commandments, and the tribute as a sign of their universal lordship and such royal dues and services as it might befit them to give; both parties swearing to fulfill everything agreed upon, with a pact concluded and contracted forever, inviolably.

The reason for this final part, of those contained in the order of natural and divine law, is this. Because natural reason dictates and teaches that any free people or nation that resolves to subject itself to the governance, jurisdiction, and principality of some person or persons, and in order to make itself subject by binding its persons to the said fidelity — which according to the jurists is a kind of servitude — and to fulfill the other rights and burdens that follow from such subjection, may request and settle upon whatever conditions it wishes, provided they are not against natural reason, and especially if they are favorable to the public good. For each private person, wishing to alienate his own property, may by that same natural reason set down whatever laws and conditions seem good to him, provided they are reasonable, because he does no wrong or harm to anyone. Therefore, it is far more lawful and natural that a man giving himself — and still more so a kingdom or any community, and even more so a world like that one — and subjecting himself to one to whom he was not subject, should be able to request and set down whatever laws and conditions seem to him most wholesome for the good of his commonwealth and the preservation of his liberty; and the other party is bound to observe them by natural law or right. All of this is proved by C. mandati, L. in remandata, where it is said that each person is the administrator, disposer, and arbiter of his own affairs; and in cap. 1 de probatio this obligation of the prince is treated at length.

These are the principal elements, among others, that the order of natural and divine law contains, which in this matter of the Indies, and especially for the justification and strengthening of the supreme and universal principality that the kings of Castile and León, by the institution or donation of the Apostolic See, claim to have and to hold over that Indian world, necessarily ought to have been observed by the Spaniards with complete and entire rigor, without a single one being lacking. Of this order of natural law in general one finds treatment in the Clementine Pastoralis, and there Giovanni d'Imola, De re iudicata; and the doctor canonists in the cap. in causis, de re iudicata; and in L. princeps, ff. De legib. 9; and in L. prohibitum and in L. iustas and in L. defensionis facultas, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10.
